To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) perceived usefulness can be measured from target users who are familiar with a new system's functionality but have not had hands-on usage experience, 2) such preprototype measures are predictive of usage intentions, and 3) such preprototype assessments of usefulness can be obtained at the earliest stages of system development, before building a prototype.
preprototype usefulness assessments are stable over time, are behaviorally predictive in the workplace, and are significantly correlated with postprototype hands-on based usefulness assessments.

(a) stable and predictive usefulness perceptions can be obtained from prospective users who have not had hands-on usage experiences with a new system, and (b) such perceptions are predictive of usage intentions, usage behavior, and system performance up to six months following workplace implementation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to improve software development project management by identifying and testing the requirements of prospective users of a new system during the earliest stages possible in the development cycle.
the development of new information technology (IT) and how to make it more useful and easier to use.
the problem of how to best assess user acceptance of information systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the context of a new information system, the present findings demonstrate that it is not necessary for prospective users to have direct hands-on usage of a system to provide stable and predictive assessments that are useful for system design.

the present research provides a strong empirical basis for believing that preprototype testing of a system's usefulness is a viable alternative to postprototype testing, and may be more valuable in terms of the cost/benefit tradeoffs that must be made in the system development context.

, although preprototype testing of a new information system's ease of use is not feasible, preprototype testing of its perceived usefulness can provide a valuable source of information for developers and users alike.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
user acceptance testing can be done earlier than is currently done, but that it is not as easy as one might hope.
the present findings provide a strong foundation for future research on preprototype user acceptance of new information systems.
preprototype usefulness assessments can provide a reliable and predictive indicator of workplace usage behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the traditional wisdom among system developers is only partially true: it is true that users must have direct experience with at least some form of the new system before they will be able to make accurate assessments of its ease of use.
the conventional assumption that hands-on experience is required to predict usage intentions and behaviors is only partially correct.
it is possible to predict future usage of a system from information about the system's functionality that is captured before users have had direct hands-on experience.
